steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper on referring image segmentation that introduces Mask Grounding, an auxiliary training task for fine-grained visual grounding, and our MagNet network. Explain the task and its key challenge, where existing methods fall short, our approach and results, and list the main contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Image segmentation tasks and Referring Image Segmentation (RIS)
- Key challenge: modality gap and language-image alignment
- Limitations of existing methods
- Mask Grounding auxiliary task
- Cross-modal alignment, MagNet and results
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Segmentation tasks and RIS
  - deep learning improved semantic, instance, panoptic segmentation
  - group pixels under fixed pre-defined categories; differ in granularity of grouping semantics
  - RIS: challenging multi-modal task; understand fine-grained language expression + pixel-level correspondence to referred object
  - attention: human-robot interaction, interactive image editing, advanced driver-assistance systems
- Key challenge
  - reduce modality gap between language and image features
  - need effective alignment of expression and pixels to highlight target
  - ideal: high similarity same object, low similarity different objects
  - non-trivial: expressions highly complex and diverse
- Existing methods (Fig. 2)
  - new losses or new architectures/modules for alignment
  - limitation 1: sentence-level language features
  - limitation 2: no explicit supervision for fine-grained visual grounding
  - language features become noisy anchors for RIS prediction
  - struggle with intricate reasoning over inter-object relationships, clauses in rare/ambiguous contexts (Fig. 1)
- Mask Grounding
  - auxiliary task: correspondence between masked textual tokens and matching visual objects
  - training: randomly masked tokens, predict identities
  - uses visual + segmentation info, not only textual context
  - must link masked tokens to visual objects -> fine-grained visual grounding
  - validated with extensive ablations; universal, improves prior RIS methods
- MagNet and results
  - cross-modal alignment loss + alignment module, bridge modality gap holistically
  - MagNet (Mask-grounded Network): new records on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, G-Ref
  - up to 2.48 points overall IoU
  - visual examination: works in complex scenarios
- Contributions
  - 1. shortcomings of SOTA RIS: lack of fine-grained visual grounding
  - 2. Mask Grounding; rigorous ablations
  - 3. MagNet with alignment loss + module; new SOTA

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has improved the performance of vision algorithms a lot on many image segmentation tasks, like semantic segmentation, instance segmentation and panoptic segmentation. In these tasks image pixels have to be grouped under a fixed set of pre-defined categories, and the tasks mainly differ in how fine-grained the grouping semantics need to be. Unlike these uni-modal segmentation tasks, Referring Image Segmentation (RIS) is a challenging multi-modal task. An algorithm for RIS has to understand fine-grained human language expression and at the same time make correct pixel-level correspondence to the referred object. Recently RIS has received a lot of research attention because it could improve human-robot interaction, interactive image editing and advanced driver-assistance systems.

The key challenge in RIS is how to reduce the modality gap between language and image features. To deal with this we need effective alignment between the given language expression and the corresponding image pixels, so that the referred target is highlighted. Ideally, if pixel-wise language-image alignment is robust, language and image features should have high feature similarity when they refer to the same object and low feature similarity when they refer to different objects. But this alignment is not easy to achieve, because the language expression can be very complex and diverse.

As shown in Fig. 2, most existing methods focus on designing new losses or new network architectures/modules to improve language-image alignment. They have made progress, but two general limitations remain. First, they tend to use sentence-level language features for language-image alignment. Second, they often do not have explicit training supervision for fine-grained visual grounding. Because of this their language features become noisy anchors for RIS prediction, and this stops them from learning fine-grained visual grounding effectively. So these models have difficulty with referring expressions that need intricate reasoning over complex inter-object relationships, or that contain clauses used in rare or ambiguous contexts, like the examples in Fig. 1.

- Mask Grounding
  - auxiliary task: masked textual tokens <-> matching visual objects
  - predict randomly masked tokens using visual + segmentation info, not just text context
  - forces correct linkage -> fine-grained visual grounding
  - extensive ablations; universal, improves prior RIS methods
- MagNet and results
  - cross-modal alignment loss + alignment module
  - MagNet (Mask-grounded Network): new records on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, G-Ref; up to 2.48 points overall IoU
  - works well in complex scenarios
- Contributions: shortcomings of SOTA; Mask Grounding; MagNet

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has improved the performance of vision algorithms a lot on many image segmentation tasks, like semantic segmentation, instance segmentation and panoptic segmentation. In these tasks image pixels have to be grouped under a fixed set of pre-defined categories, and the tasks mainly differ in how fine-grained the grouping semantics need to be. Unlike these uni-modal segmentation tasks, Referring Image Segmentation (RIS) is a challenging multi-modal task. An algorithm for RIS has to understand fine-grained human language expression and at the same time make correct pixel-level correspondence to the referred object. Recently RIS has received a lot of research attention because it could improve human-robot interaction, interactive image editing and advanced driver-assistance systems.

The key challenge in RIS is how to reduce the modality gap between language and image features. To deal with this we need effective alignment between the given language expression and the corresponding image pixels, so that the referred target is highlighted. Ideally, if pixel-wise language-image alignment is robust, language and image features should have high feature similarity when they refer to the same object and low feature similarity when they refer to different objects. But this alignment is not easy to achieve, because the language expression can be very complex and diverse.

As shown in Fig. 2, most existing methods focus on designing new losses or new network architectures/modules to improve language-image alignment. They have made progress, but two general limitations remain. First, they tend to use sentence-level language features for language-image alignment. Second, they often do not have explicit training supervision for fine-grained visual grounding. Because of this their language features become noisy anchors for RIS prediction, and this stops them from learning fine-grained visual grounding effectively. So these models have difficulty with referring expressions that need intricate reasoning over complex inter-object relationships, or that contain clauses used in rare or ambiguous contexts, like the examples in Fig. 1.

To solve this, we introduce a new auxiliary task called Mask Grounding, which explicitly teaches our model to make fine-grained correspondence between masked textual tokens and the visual objects they match. During training, our model sees randomly masked textual tokens and has to predict what they are. The model does not rely only on the surrounding textual context to predict these tokens, but integrates visual and segmentation information as well. This is key for the model to predict accurately, because it has to find and establish the correct link between the masked tokens and their visual objects. By learning this, our model becomes very good at fine-grained visual grounding, which is very much wanted. We validate the efficacy of Mask Grounding empirically with extensive ablation experiments. We also show that Mask Grounding is universal and can be used directly on prior RIS methods to give significant improvements.

Besides Mask Grounding, we also design a cross-modal alignment loss and an alignment module to bridge the modality gap holistically. With all of these, our resulting MagNet (Mask-grounded Network) sets new records and significantly outperforms previous SOTA methods on all key datasets (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and G-Ref). Our method outperforms these SOTA methods consistently, by large margins of up to 2.48 points in overall IoU. Looking at MagNet's predictions visually also supports our claim and shows that our method works well in complex scenarios.

Our main contributions are:

- 1. We point out the shortcomings in recent state-of-the-art (SOTA) RIS algorithms, namely the lack of fine-grained visual grounding.

- 2. We introduce the Mask Grounding auxiliary task, a new method for improving fine-grained visual grounding in existing RIS algorithms. Its effectiveness is validated with rigorous ablation studies.

- 3. Using Mask Grounding, together with our cross-modal alignment loss and an alignment module, we present MagNet (Mask-grounded Network), a new SOTA network for RIS.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has greatly improved the performance of vision algorithms on many image segmentation tasks, such as semantic segmentation [1,2], instance segmentation [3,4,5,6] and panoptic segmentation [7,8]. These tasks require grouping image pixels under a fixed set of pre-defined categories and differ mainly in the granularity of the grouping semantics. In contrast to these uni-modal segmentation tasks, Referring Image Segmentation (RIS) [9,10] is a challenging multi-modal task that requires an algorithm to simultaneously understand fine-grained human language expressions and make correct pixel-level correspondence to the referred object. Recently, it has gained widespread research attention due to its potential to improve human-robot interaction [11], interactive image editing [12,13] and advanced driver-assistance systems [14].

The key challenge in RIS lies in reducing the modality gap between language and image features [15,16,17]. To tackle this challenge, we need an effective alignment between a given language expression and the corresponding image pixels to highlight the referred target. Ideally, with robust pixel-wise language-image alignment, language and image features should have high similarity when referring to the same object and low similarity when referring to different objects. However, achieving such alignment is non-trivial, because language expressions can be highly complex and diverse.

As depicted in Fig. 2, prevailing methods mainly focus on devising innovative losses [17,18] or introducing new network architectures/modules [15,19,16,20,21] to bolster language-image alignment. Despite their advances, two overarching limitations persist. First, these approaches tend to rely on sentence-level language features for language-image alignment. Second, they often lack explicit training supervision for fine-grained visual grounding. As a result, their language features become noisy anchors for RIS prediction [22,20], which inhibits effective learning of fine-grained visual grounding. Consequently, such models struggle to interpret referring expressions that require intricate reasoning across complex inter-object relationships or that contain clauses used in rare or ambiguous contexts, as exemplified in Fig. 1.

To address this challenge, we introduce a novel Mask Grounding auxiliary task that explicitly teaches our model to make fine-grained correspondence between masked textual tokens and their matching visual objects. Specifically, during training our model encounters randomly masked textual tokens and has to predict their identities. Rather than relying solely on the surrounding textual context, our model integrates both visual and segmentation information to predict these tokens. This integration is pivotal for accurate prediction, as the model must discern and establish the correct link between the masked tokens and their corresponding visual objects. Learning to do so ensures that our model acquires strong proficiency in the highly-coveted fine-grained visual grounding. The efficacy of Mask Grounding is validated empirically with extensive ablation experiments. We also show that Mask Grounding is universal and can be directly applied to prior RIS methods to bring significant improvements.

In addition to Mask Grounding, we design a cross-modal alignment loss and an alignment module to holistically bridge the modality gap. With all these enhancements, our resulting MagNet (Mask-grounded Network) sets new records, significantly outperforming previous SOTA methods across all key datasets (RefCOCO [23], RefCOCO+ [23] and G-Ref [24,25]). Notably, our method consistently outperforms these SOTA methods by large margins of up to 2.48 points in overall IoU. A visual examination of MagNet’s predictions reinforces this claim and shows that our method works well in complex scenarios.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

- 1. We highlight the shortcomings of recent state-of-the-art (SOTA) RIS algorithms, pinpointing their lack of fine-grained visual grounding.

- 2. We introduce the Mask Grounding auxiliary task, a novel method for enhancing fine-grained visual grounding in existing RIS algorithms, and validate its effectiveness through rigorous ablation studies.

- 3. Using Mask Grounding together with our specially designed cross-modal alignment loss and an accompanying alignment module, we present MagNet (Mask-grounded Network), a new SOTA network for RIS.
